opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Emily, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I run operations for a logistics company: warehouses, transport, the lot. I also lead our automation programme, so I'm on the other side of a lot of these questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is table stakes now. If you don't use it in your bids and your planning, you don't win contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's honestly what I believe. In this picture it's a productivity tool and we squeeze a few percent out of it. Nothing that changes my world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep rolling it out in route planning and labour forecasting, and make sure every site manager actually uses the dashboards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This is business as usual for me.

S0.say: AI is table stakes. If you don't use it in your bids and planning, you don't win contracts.
S0.think: It's a productivity tool. We squeeze a few percent out of it and my world doesn't change.
S0.do: Keeps rolling AI into route planning and labour forecasting, and makes every site manager use the dashboards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow adoption is a gift for the companies that move early. That's us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's slow, the advantage goes to whoever builds the skills first. I'm good at this, and I'd be one of the people others hire to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the board for a bigger automation budget and hire two or three strong data people before everyone else wants them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly pleased, if I'm honest.

S1.say: Slow adoption is a gift for companies that move early, and that's us.
S1.think: The edge goes to whoever builds the skills first. I'm good at this, so I'd be the one others want to hire.
S1.do: Pushes the board for a bigger automation budget and hires two or three strong data people early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly: we'll redeploy where we can and we'll be transparent with our people. That's the line, and we'd try to mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a big chunk of our office staff, the planners, schedulers and customer service teams, wouldn't be needed. I'd be the one signing off on it. That's uncomfortable, but it's my job, and if we don't do it a competitor will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the restructure in the office teams within twelve months, set up a small retraining track for the strongest people and win two new contracts on the cost savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine for me. Not great about the people part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try to mean the transparency line. What would get in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Timing. You can't tell people about cuts before the board signs off, and by then it's nearly done. So 'transparent' tends to mean 'quick'.

S2.say: We'll redeploy where we can and be transparent with our people.
S2.think: Most of our planners and schedulers wouldn't be needed and I'd sign it off. Uncomfortable, but if we don't, a competitor will.
S2.do: Runs the office restructure within a year, sets up a retraining track for the strongest staff and wins new contracts on the savings.
S2.feel: Fine personally, not great about the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say leaders have a duty to manage this responsibly, and that we're investing in our people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the first one where I look at my own job. If AI matches a skilled professional, it can plan a network as well as my team, maybe as well as me. I still think I'd be one of the last to go, because someone has to answer to clients and the board. But I'm less sure than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the face of the transformation to the board and to clients. I'd also move some of our savings out of shares into property and cash, because booms end. And I'd talk to the kids about what they study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd notice myself checking.

S3.say: Leaders have a duty to manage this responsibly, and we're investing in our people.
S3.think: AI could plan a network as well as my team, maybe as well as me. I think I'd be among the last to go, but I'm less sure than I'd like.
S3.do: Makes herself the face of the change to the board and clients, moves some savings out of shares into property and cash, and talks to her kids about study choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest change in logistics in a generation, and we intend to lead it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oddly, this one's better for me than the last. Every warehouse in the country would need to be rebuilt around robots, and somebody has to plan that, run it and deal with the unions and the safety issues. That's exactly what I've been doing for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the board in month one with a full robot rollout plan and ask for the money. I'd hire engineers and safety people. And honestly, I'd probably get calls from bigger firms, and I'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Energised, even. The people side still bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture made you uneasy, and this one adds more change. Why do you feel better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in the last one my skills were the thing being copied. In this one, my skills are what everybody suddenly needs. Physical rollouts are messy. Messy is where I'm worth something.

S4.say: This is the biggest change in logistics in a generation, and we intend to lead it.
S4.think: This is better for me than the last one. Every warehouse needs rebuilding around robots, and planning that is exactly what I've done for years.
S4.do: Brings the board a full robot rollout plan in month one, hires engineers and safety staff, and listens to offers from bigger firms.
S4.feel: Energised, though the people side still bothers her.
